Thank you, Mr. Speaker. At this point it is well for us to understand, in general terms at least, the different capitals with which we have to work. Adam Smith understood this when he realized that labour and land were not sufficient; that in a mechanized world capital is necessary. Today, as automation takes over, how much more necessary is it for us to understand the basic purpose of capital if we are to survive at all as a free way of life.
We have tax capital. Tax capital is the money which the tax collector takes from your pockets, my pockets and the pockets of all Canadians to pay for the services which government renders. Governments have no source of capital except as they take it from us, the taxpayers, or as they use our credit to borrow money to make up deficits. I think the sooner we understand, the better. I suggest to hon. members of the house on this side that the sooner we remember that the only money governments have to spend is tax money, the better off it is going to be for our economy. You cannot get something for nothing when it comes to paying the cost of services of government.
Second, there is commercial capital, which has better been called production capital. This is the capital which comes from our savings and which is rightfully used for the development of our resources and the carrying on of our commerce. This is the kind of capital that
The Address-Mr. Thompson earns a profit. There is nothing wrong with profit. Some of our hon. friends would make "profit" a dirty word. Profit is nothing more or less than the earnings of the invested capital as it produces our needs.
The trouble in our country today is that our production capital lies idle when it should be at work developing our country. If 25 per cent of this type capital today that lies idle were put to work, there would be no shortage of capital and we would not have to be crying for capital from outside the country.
I should here like to mention a third type of capital which is most important to us right now. This is public capital. Public capital is capital which is used to construct and make possible our public projects which do not earn a profit. I am thinking of schools, hospitals, highways, bridges and canals. This is the type of capital we must have to finance the capital development of our public or social needs.
We in this corner of the house maintain that this capital should not come from the commercial market. It should come from a municipal development bank as an integral part of the Bank of Canada. May we remember here that such capital does not earn a profit. Do we earn a profit on schools, highways, hospitals or canals? No. Instead, it facilitates a service. Public capital under the present system is drawn off the commercial market at high rates of interest. As a result, the cost to the taxpayer of all public developments in this country is more than double the cost of the actual construction itself. As an example, board sidewalks costing $100,000 in 1912 cost the Vancouver taxpayer $345,000 by the time the final payment was made in 1962. The paradox of this is that those sidewalks never earned a cent of profit and they rotted away more than 30 years ago.
The real purpose of a municipal development bank and not that of a municipal fund, which just takes more money to redistribute to the others, is to supply the credit which is necessary for the construction of our public capital works and this is one of the most urgent needs at this moment in our economy because unless this type of expansion can go forward this winter we shall be facing one of the grimmest winters we have experienced for many a year. While I do not claim to be a prophet nor a son of a prophet, I am sure that by next spring we shall have 20 per cent of our work force unemployed, together with a cost of living higher than it has ever been. This is something we shall have to face in this house in this parliamentary week. Canada stands at a crossroads in her history and the crisis

The Address-Mr. Thompson centres right here in this house. It is essential that we should face up to it and meet the responsibility which is before us. What does this involve? On the part of the government-and I think this is very important-it must be remembered that this is a house of minorities. They must acknowledge that they do not have the trust and confidence of the Canadian people generally; they form a government only because they have the largest minority group. The government and its supporters must recognize that the policies and program which they have followed in the last five years are responsible for the loss of public support and therefore they must be willing to give heed to some of the recommendations from the other parties whose combined public support represents nearly two thirds of the electorate.
The Liberals, as the official opposition, must recognize that the situation in Canada today is not a normal set of circumstances but a national emergency. Statesmanship requires that they should forego their traditional political procedures and give precedence to a position dictated by the national interest.
We in this corner are not responsible for the government's decisions. We will use this opportunity to give leadership and a practical demonstration of statesmanship as against the jockeying for partisan advantages which the prevailing situation invites and which is so characteristic of both the larger parties.
What is our practical approach? To be practical it is essential that we look at the facts. The confused situation facing parliament obviates clear thinking and brings into focus two specific issues. First, with regard to external affairs, a realistic program is needed to solve the balance of payments problem. Obviously, temporary emergency measures cannot solve anything. We cannot expect to return to normal conditions and progress if we maintain these emergency measures. It is essential that external credits be granted, using the Bank of Canada to increase exports for the good of all the people. To increase exports is a more logical approach than the curtailing of imports except when domestic production will not increase consumer costs.
Internally, there is an urgent need to create circumstances which will assure a buoyant and confident internal economy. We need: adequate capital for industrial expansion; adequate consumer purchasing power, and adequate social measures for large-scale municipal growth and improvements.
Thus, I think we must rise above those things which divide us politically, to the level of the statesmanship which the nation needs at this time. Let us have a few months at


least free from partisan considerations. Let us keep Canada first. Our party recognizes and acknowledges the facts with respect to its own position in parliament. No one has the confidence of a majority. Collectively, we all represent the public will. In this regard there is a particular responsibility resting on the government party, since they form the government. Social Credit is determined to follow the role of statesmanship. This is the only approach. I appeal to each party, to each individual member of this house, to consider their responsibility. If this responsibility is rejected, the only outcome would be a national crisis.
In five short years we shall be celebrating the hundredth anniversary of our nationhood. Before this historic milestone is reached, the people of this land will have to reach a decision. They will have to decide whether they will continue to blunder along the path of confusion and indecision. This decision may well be as vital as was the decision which first united the foundling provinces of this great nation. Shall we continue down the road we have been travelling to the inevitable economic and financial crisis to which our debt system has been taking us? Shall we continue to believe in a system which says we never had it so good and then, the next week, have to tell the people that the country is going broke? Shall we have confidence in a system which told us in 1957 and again in 1962 that we were in the midst of a period of economic expansion only to wake up to find tight money and high interest rates holding us back?
Would it be better to turn to the left and sacrifice the remaining vestige of freedom and dependence, first to the false hope of socialism and later to communism which is the socialist's ultimate destiny? True, it would be an alternative to the old way admitted even by those who profess free enterprise but who, in their expediency, have become the apologists of the very philosophies which they preach.
Or shall we turn to what is right and set our feet on a new path which will lead this nation into an era of prosperity and freedom with opportunity for all? This is the problem to which hon. members must find an answer as we face our joint responsibilities in parliament toward the needs of our nation at this time.

I think my hon. friend opposite understands what I mean. I do not like using the word the Prime Minister used. The limited time at my disposal does not permit me the luxury of gnawing on the bone of partisan trivialities. Therefore, I intend to take the time at my disposal to present a synopsis of our program to the house. Other members of this group will deal in more detail with particular aspects of the throne speech and our program, will give a thoughtful analysis of the economic situation as we see it and of our proposals, and make certain criticisms, comments and observations on the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), and my hon. friend opposite.
However, before proceeding I must say this. I think a good many members will agree with me that a considerable portion of this very important debate has been considerably below par. I think we have a definite responsibility to the institution of parliament and to the Canadian people. So far as this group is concerned, it accepts its responsibility. It will continue to do all it can to maintain the dignity of parliament, promote respect for parliament, and make it function more efficiently for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party have tried their best to receive the speech from the throne with a broad mind and in as charitable a fashion as possible. It has been very hard. We have listened carefully for any hint or suggestion of protective measures to deal with the many serious problems which face Canadians today. I must admit, however, that looking for positive measures in this throne speech requires a degree of optimism equal to that of the man who looks for eggs in a cuckoo clock. Government promises in the throne speech remind me of the huckleberry crop in British Columbia this year. In April the huckleberry bushes were
The Address-Mr. Herridge replete with blossom; blossom was on the huckleberries everywhere in profusion. Then we had a few chilly days in May, and we have not had any huckleberries in September. I think that illustrates very well the government's promises and the indications of what the government intend to do so far as this speech is concerned. I think it is quite safe to say that the majority of Canadians generally now realize that the government's performance has fallen far short of its promises since 1957. Anyone who has read the record throughout the years will fairly agree with that, I think. Government ineptitude, lack of purpose and lack of direction have been repeatedly demonstrated. My time does not permit me to go into numerous illustrations, but seeing that the subject has been mentioned this evening, I want to bring one illustration to the house which I think shows this perfectly. Time will permit me only to give this one illustration of the government's lack of purpose, policy and program, namely, the tragic desertion of principle and capitulation to the premier of British Columbia in the matter of the Columbia river treaty. I wish to point that out. It is a most unusual circumstance. Never before in Canadian history have we had cabinet ministers telling the public a few months before that such a course of action would betray the interests of the Canadian people, who then turned around later and did just that.
Now, two paragraphs in the speech from the throne concern us. They are that:
It is hoped that arrangements will soon be completed that will make it possible to submit for your approval the Columbia river treaty and the legislation required in parliament to implement it.
The second paragraph is:

In the main the throne speech concerns itself with economic affairs. Once again we find the Conservative government can look at exactly the same evidence as everybody else and yet come up with an observation all their own. It is very clever of them. The rest of us look at the dominion bureau of statistics figures which show that average annual unemployment in Canada has hovered around 7 per cent of the labour force during the last four years and that last year the per capita real gross national product was less than it was in 1956, and we arrive at the conclusion that this is a very shoddy performance.
For example, a recent report by President Kennedy's committee on unemployment revealed that the United States has the highest unemployment of any non-Communist industrial country, with the exception of Canada. I noted that the leader of the official opposition mentioned that matter in his speech. Canadians are noticing it. On this matter I am getting letters cut out of papers and underlined. The facts are being impressed on a good many Canadians. The government, however, interprets exactly the same set of data to mean that the economy has moved ahead sharply. This seems very odd to me and to the other members of our party, but doubtless these are mysteries which mere mortals like myself cannot hope to comprehend.
It came as no surprise to most of us that the government is determined to continue the austerity program. What I think staggers the imagination of anyone who thinks seriously about these things is this. The government thinks it can provide a million new jobs over the next five years and keep the austerity program at the same time. Tight money and reduced government spending are bound to increase unemployment and further restrict economic growth. These are, from our point of view, exactly the wrong policies to adopt in our present economic circumstances. All across the country the cry has been taken up that the time has come for Canadians to tighten their belts. In an economy such as ours we believe this is dangerous and misleading nonsense. Belt tightening policies might be called for if we already had full employment, were producing at full capacity, and were in danger of inflation. But to tighten our belts now can only prolong and aggravate
The Address-Mr. Herridge the high unemployment and sluggish economic growth which have been this country's shame for the past six years.
I just want to deal with this aspect of the matter. Let us consider the tight money policy for example. With interest rates of 5 per cent and 6 per cent the provinces and municipalities will be unable to borrow the funds they need for essential social capital investments. Everyone knows that all across Canada there is a tremendous need for social capital of all kinds for schools, houses, hospitals, roads, bridges, public power, slum clearance, urban renewal, parks, recreation centres and the like. The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has brought these matters before the government on more than one occasion and I have discussed this matter with officials of the federation. Not only are these projects desperately needed by our society now; they are also capable of creating thousands of jobs for unemployed Canadians and for those thousands more who will enter the labour force over the next few years. There are thousands coming into our labour force every year. Many of these projects are the responsibility of the provincial and municipal governments. On behalf of this group I wish to emphasize that in order to carry out investments of this magnitude they must borrow money. But when interest rates are as high as they are now under the tight money policy, we find this situation.
I wish my hon. friend the leader of the aggregation opposite me had been in this house when their former leader, Mr. Low, used to talk about the tight money policy. The hon. gentleman sang a very different tune from that sung by his predecessor in the years gone by. When these things are abandoned, thousands upon thousands of potential jobs will be lost to the Canadian economy. There is no question about that matter. Tight money also restricts the investment plans of small businesses. Small business is noticing this throughout the country and small business is beginning to turn towards this party of social progress to come to its rescue. More and more people are beginning to realize that we are the ones who believe in the mixed economy, public ownership, co-operative ownership and legitimate free enterprise, particularly small business.

Mr. Speaker, when I was enjoying my dinner and noticing the large number of people who were enjoying their dinner in comfort, I could not help thinking of the millions in the world who go to bed hungry every night, and of the task we have to set things right both at home and abroad, a task that will tax our humanity, integrity, intelligence and industry.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when we rose at six o'clock I was questioning the statement that the government's policy would create a million jobs in five years. I said I would like to know how. I may say that equally disastrous is the government's determination to make large cutbacks in government expenditures. From our point of view it will be particularly harmful if those cutbacks take place in public works and social capital. This is precisely the sector of our economy where a much higher level of investment is needed and which has the greatest potential for creating new employment. This is a self-liquidating investment which returns something to our society throughout the years. A cutback in expenditures here will depress employment directly.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, it is not only this government's projects that will cause a loss of jobs. It must be remembered that each employee on these projects will be spending part of his wages and salary on the goods produced by private industry, thus expanding employment and production in that sector of the economy as well. Therefore, the members of this party say that when the government makes giant cutbacks in government expenditures it costs jobs both in public and private industry. We fail to see how we are going to get economic growth, rising employment and production as promised in the throne speech on this basis.
The austerity program is diametrically opposed to economic expansion. When the government talks about using austerity to promote prosperity, I am reminded of those governments in Canada and the United States, as well as Britain, during the thirties, that thought the way to solve the paradox of


poverty in the midst of plenty was to get rid of the plenty. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a great many members in this house can remember the policies of former president Hoover, of Britain going off the gold standard, and the consequent unemployment in Great Britain and then in Canada. We remember exactly the same austerity program under former prime minister Bennett which created great hardship when the stability of money was of more concern than the welfare of human beings.
We in the New Democratic party are convinced that you can only get full employment and economic expansion through a system of democratic planning. Now, you know, planning has become very popular. I recall some years ago the leader of the group opposite rising in this house and saying-and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) remembers the occasion, and you will find it in the record- that anybody who suggests economic planning in Canada is suggesting reducing the Canadian people to slavery. Well, we have had an impact on thinking people in Canada. Planning has become quite respectable. Even the heads of big corporations realize there has to be a measure of planning, and so does this Conservative government realize it. But our point is that this economic planning must be under the direction of this house which is responsible to the people of Canada, and not the directors of big corporations.
We note, Mr. Speaker, that the throne speech makes special mention of a national economic development board, but as usual the wording used by this government in throne speeches is very vague in relation to the jurisdiction and powers that this board will have. I must say that from past experience we are very suspicious of the exact meaning of this wording. We are waiting with interest for some elaboration of the proposal, some details of what is actually meant. Will it be a serious effort at economic planning in Canada on the part of this government, in co-operation with provincial governments and other levels of government, or will it turn out to be a second cousin to that mammoth hoax the productivity council? This is the question we are asking.
The New Democratic party has made clear its policy on economic planning. We have also made it clear what we do not regard as planning. For example, planning does not mean mere economic forecasting. It does not mean just a review of what is already happening in the economy. It does not mean a mere announcement of economic goals. It does not mean the mere lumping together of the separate programs of government departments. Finally, it does not mean simply the

exchange of information and advice between the government and a board of advisers. It goes far beyond that.
Democratic economic planning, Mr. Speaker, as understood in this party and by an increasing number of Canadians at this time consists of four things. In the first place, it is an account of the possibilities in Canada. It is an estimate of what the economy can do, of what it might do this year and next year and in all the years of the foreseeable future. The range of choice is enormous when one applies his thoughts to this question. How much education are we prepared to provide today? We in this group believe that every Canadian child, regardless of where it lives or the economic circumstances of its parents, is entitled to all the education of which it is capable of taking advantage at the expense of us all. How much northern development should there be? Now, our northern development would extend beyond that unconventional project of the government's last year in the Yukon, but which had a great d^al of news value. I am all for preserving these historical sites, but we have to set our "sights" much higher than that. I mean that in several senses.
What kind of industrial investment is required in this country? What combinations of all these things are possible? Now, Mr. Speaker, we have the mechanisms, we have the services in federal government. They have them in the provincial governments. You would be surprised at the number of persons in private industry and in local organizations who would be willing to cooperate with the government if it had a purpose, a plan which was prepared and in which they were asked to co-operate. We simply fail to take advantage of the reservoir of goodwill that exists amongst the Canadian people. I am one of those who believe that we have to provide the morale equivalent to that prevailing in wartime; we have to stir the people to believe that they are proud of this country. I am a Canadian and proud of it. We have got to get them thinking of national problems and get their co-operation in national projects and objectives.
I think all of us realize that in an unplanned economy there is a feeling of inevitability about what happens. Indeed, I meet people today who ask "What is the use"? because they realize they are capable of starting this going and getting it in motion, and that sort of thing, but this inevitability is taken as an excuse for poor economic performance by governments, and by private industry in some cases, but a planned economy shows how wide and rich the possibilities are from which we can choose. This will be democracy in action.
The Address-Mr. Herridge Here we will have people applying themselves to the maintenance of political freedom and working at the same time towards the extension of our economic freedom.
I suppose I should interject at this point that we would set up a planning board, consisting of economists, engineers and other experts whose job it would be constantly to conduct studies of the Canadian economy, draw up goals and priorities and the means for implementing them, and report regularly to the government.
In the second place a democratic economic plan is the discovery of what people actually want. It is not just making them want a lot of the tinselled, useless things peddled to them today which create standards for false values. We would find out what the people should want, and do want in the majority of cases. I represent a constituency of good solid Canadians, 50 per cent rural and 50 per cent industrial, but I find that the great majority of people do not understand what are the sound values in life, what are the things worth looking for and what are the things worth acquiring. We should find out what they want. We should give them a chance to express themselves instead of flooding them with the tinsel things on which they are asked to spend their money today.
In the New Democratic program we call for the establishment of an economic advisory council, representing business, labour, farmers and consumers. We say that a part of the function of this council would be to keep the government informed about how the people want their economy to perform and what they want it to produce. Of course the first things are the necessities of life for everybody.

Finally, democratic economic planning is the deliberate determined use of intervention and direction to attain the goals of the plan. We believe it is time that those responsible to the people determined the direction of investment, the rate of investment and the development of our natural resources. This is where our concept of planning departs significantly from planning as it is understood by the other political parties. The leader of the Liberal party, for example, bases his party's belief only in advisory planning. It was rather disappointing to hear this as I thought we had influenced him more than that during the last parliament.
Unless the government is prepared to intervene in economic affairs to ensure that the people's choices are translated into achievement, then any planning institutions the government set up would be next to useless. Democratic choice is denied in the unplanned, so-called free market economy. People do not choose unemployment and declining per capita production, but these things have happened just because of our unplanned system. The people want more social capital, more roads, more schools and hospitals, but there is no way in which they can express their demand for such goods in the private market, in the way that they can express their demand for an automobile or an electric toaster.
In the private market economy there is a wide range of choice denied to consumers. Unless planning institutions are created, and unless the government is prepared to intervene in the economy to ensure that the recommended and planned goals are achieved, then the government is not engaged in economic planning at all. Without planning, the performance of our economy will grow worse and social and economic democracy will be denied to the majority of Canadians.
Some may ask whether economic planning of the kind this party believes in has any relevance to Canada's present economic problems. We are convinced that it has. A New Democratic government would use its planning institutions to promote economic growth, full employment and a higher standard of living, and may I say that we look upon a higher standard of living as a development towards a higher social and spiritual life, because with a higher standard of living insecurity will have been removed.
This would lead us to policies which are diametrically opposed to the policies of the government as outlined in the speech from the throne. In particular it would lead us to

reject tight money and any cut-back in government expenditure on public works. We would replace high interest rates by low, long term interest rates to encourage investment by the provinces and municipalities, and by small businessmen and home builders. An easy money policy of this kind would provide new employment and give our sluggish economic growth a shot in the arm. It is the wrong policy to reduce government spending at this time.
This party is not afraid of budget deficits when these are part of a plan to promote full employment and economic growth. The reason the very large deficits of the present government have not been successful in this regard is that these deficits have arisen as the result of mistake, and not as the result of planning. They have arisen largely as a result of our sluggish economy failing to yield the expected tax revenues, but properly and deliberately planned deficit spending is necessary to promote full employment at the present time. If people do not believe this then I would refer them to the economies of countries in western Europe.
Instead of reducing government expenditures, we would launch a massive program of public spending on social capital, on roads, hospital, public housing, transportation, education, natural resource development, urban renewal, slum clearance and so on. Not only would this fill a serious gap in the range of goods and services available to the Canadian economy but it would generate new incomes and thousands upon thousands of jobs, both in the public and private sectors of the economy.
In the days to come other members of this group will deal with our proposals in greater detail. We intend to put our proposals logically before the house. They are the result of considerable discussion and co-operation with economists, engineers, research people and other authorities, and we are putting them forward realizing that they are the result of the application of intelligence to the problems that face us today.
In addition to the measures I have already mentioned, other members will explain why the New Democratic party favours abandoning the pegged exchange rate of the Canadian dollar and returning to a free-floating rate, in order to meet our balance of payments difficulties without sacrificing employment and growth in the process, which a fixed rate inevitably does. They will present other suggestions for improving Canada's long-run balance of payments, and will comment on the trade and tariff policy of the present government in some detail.

Firmly convinced of the truth of those words of a great man, the Conservative party has decided to create unity under that symbol. I should like to speak for a moment on this matter that is so important to everybody I am sure in Canada. In doing so, I think back to the time years ago when I was a small boy and had a younger neighbour who at times was irritating. Occasionally I was tempted to use my slightly greater size and administer a little bit of punishment. Whenever I got him on the ground he used to say, "Now John, remember you are British". Barbara Ward, in her interesting little book written recently says this:
I suppose we are all aware of the fact that we live in the most catastrophically revolutionary age that men have ever faced.
In 1936 H.A.L. Fisher wrote from the English point of view a book entitled "A History of Europe". It was an excellent book. The preface to that book is cynical because in it he said this:
One intellectual excitement has been denied me. Men wiser and more learned than I have discerned in history a plot, a rhythm, a predetermined pattern. These harmonies are concealed from me. I can see only one emergency following upon another as wave follows upon wave.

The Address-Mr. Matheson
All he could see was the play of the contingent and the unforeseen. I think the tragedy of our time in Canada is the kind of leadership we have now. Since 1936 great things have happened and there are patterns and harmonies that can be seen by those who have eyes and wish to see. When we look at this British subject today, I think we must look at it with a bit of depth.
May I refer to some of the problems of just a few years ago in world war I which we so quickly pass over and forget. I ask this house to recall that in the battle of the Marne in August 1914, France lost approximately 300,000 men. In that great battle, which some members of this house will remember, and which is spoken of as the miracle of the Marne, France actually held the situation together in Europe. The war memorial of St. Cyr to the class of 1914 is to the class as a whole. At Verdun we had practically the massacre of the French nation in the spring of 1916. The battle of Verdun extended over seven months. Those of us who are British in our background and our traditions remember the appalling butchery at Verdun. There are many Englishmen who think of France in terms of Verdun and the heroism of Verdun. Following that you will recall there were four months of the great battle of the Somme. Germany lost 500,000 men at that battle, the British 410,000 men and the French 190,000 more men. Some people in this house have some knowledge of the events of 1917: Ypres, Passchendaele. Two of the best men in my family remain there because of those battles. Then there was Cambrai and the battles that followed.
When we look at this great British problem facing us today I ask hon. members to think of it in terms of depth of this tragic history of war. France lost one out of 28 of the population. One out of every 28 was destroyed in death in world war I. Germany lost one out of 32 and England lost one out of 57. That is one of the reasons that Wilson approached this whole situation of Europe from the standpoint of an idealist and an outsider, a man who had been a keen student of the international scene, although he was in every sense an American. He put forward 14 points which became something of a vision to the rest of the world. You remember that these 14 points included open covenants of peace; freedom of navigation, removal of economic trade barriers and a great association of nations. Wilson summed up his ideas, you will recall, at the end of world war I by saying that what we are striving for is a new international order based upon the broad and universal principles of right and justice. Historians have described Wilson as forthright and stiff. Tiger Clemenceau-they say his


belief in France was noble and sincere, but she was the only thing in which he believed. The French had suffered very grievously and they were cynics. Lloyd George was hampered by the ferocious demands of the British public. Their cry was, "Hang the Kaiser".
As we look back on that terrible time in history we can see that the spirit of the league of nations and the spirit of the treaty of Versailles were utterly incompatible. You recall, Mr. Speaker, that T. E. Lawrence, who gained his experience in the desert said that when we fought together we were thinking in terms of a new heaven and a new earth. Then he said that when we won the war and came home we found the old men came out, brought out all their old ideas and the victory escaped us. This is the situation we believe could develop today. We do not want old ideas. We do not want any old views. This is a time for new wine in new bottles. We want British vigour, British idealism and British traditions put to work in the modern world which has greater possibilities than any time in the history of mankind.
Christopher Dawson is an Oxford man who tells us that actually there has been more accomplished in the last 200 years from a standpoint of human progress, in spite of the butcheries and brutalities of recent years, than in all of recorded history before that time. Are we prepared to adjust to new situations or not?
I was mentioning, too, to this house, sir, something of the disappointment the people suffered in respect of the conclusion of world war I. Let me refer to an economist. I know some of the gentlemen on the treasury benches do not think very much of economists, but this is a man about whom we have had to think pretty seriously because he has had a great influence on events in Britain and indeed in this country, in the United States and in academic circles all over the world. I refer to J. M. Keynes. Lord Keynes was perhaps best known in early days for his book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace. You will recall that it was written at Cambridge in 1919. Let me refer this house to a few passages in this important historic book with respect to Europe, England and France.
He says that before 1870 different parts of the small continent of Europe had specialized in their own products; but, taken as a whole, it was substantially self-subsistent. He says that Europe, if she is to survive her troubles, will need so much magnanimity from America that she must herself practise it. It is useless for the allies, hot from stripping Germany and one another, to turn for help to the United States to put the states of Europe, including Germany, on to their feet again.

If the general election of December, 1918, had been fought on lines of prudent generosity instead of imbecile greed, how much better the financial prospect of Europe might now be.
Then, he goes on in this important book, which is actually one of pessimism, and he tells us that Europe consists of one of the densest aggregations of population in the history of the world. This population is accustomed to a relatively high standard of life in which, even now, some sections of it anticipate improvement rather than deterioration. He says that to succeed they must work together; they cannot possibly survive alone; that it was dangerous and destructive, for example, to take iron and steel and separate them, to put a boundary between them. He says that peace has been declared at Paris, but winter approaches. Men will have nothing to look forward to or to nourish hopes on. Who can say how much is endurable or in which direction men will seek to escape from their misfortune?
Then, he tells us that the opportunity was missed at Paris during the six months which followed the Armistice and that they will never be able to recover. He says that by a moderation of the clauses of the Versailles treaty, particularly related to coal and the exchange of iron ore there could have been a continuance of Germany's industrial life with great advantage to the production of the whole group and that a free trade union comprising the whole of central, eastern and southeastern Europe, Siberia, Turkey and the United Kingdom, Egypt and India might do a great deal for the peace and prosperity of the world.
If we read that book carefully, sir, we see actually many conclusions in it that are very similar to the conclusions that we find in Mein Kampf. The only thing is that he is looking at it from the point of view of a scholarly, broadminded Britisher, and Hitler was looking at it from the standpoint of a defeated person with a perverse psychiatric disorder. These two people looked at the same problem and actually what was predicted by Lord Keynes in 1919 came to pass. There was not the same destructive effect in Europe in world war II to armed forces but when we consider the destruction of civilians, the millions and millions of Jewish people, the many emigres of one kind and another, we must surely feel that this new thing that is happening in Europe today is something we must prayerfully consider.
I am going to ask you, perhaps, to leave that subject for a moment and look at England itself. Churchill tells us that England 27507-3-10

Barbara Ward, now Lady Jackson, an editorial writer of the Economist tells us that the most important thing about Britain's entry into Europe at this time is that Europe will then have a new outlooking attitude. We know this is the plan that Winston Churchill had for many years. He attended a meeting at The Hague in 1948, at which Leon Blum represented France, and said that the time had come for the European nations to co-operate and each give up some portion of its sovereign rights. I say that this point of view is completely incompatible with the kind of words we heard from the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), who is taking the narrow, nationalist attitude at a time when most countries in the world could benefit by the larger approach, this international approach, and particularly by the marriage between these two nations which have been the foundation of Canada-France and Great Britain.
I am not talking only about peace, although 20 years ago all we asked was the chance to come back to Canada to live and get by without further war. That has been granted us and the mistakes of Versailles have not been made this time. In large measure this was due to the Marshall plan and I only wish I had time to develop my remarks with regard to it. However, the leadership came not from Canada, not from us who are the heirs of the British tradition, but from the United States. The Marshall plan gave the world a new start and now there are great possibilities ahead for us if Britain implements its forward looking, brave policy of joining Europe.
We should look at some of the literature coming out of Germany. Ludwig Erhard has said:
Our economic task-the employment of over 12 million more people than before the war-cannot be carried through but must founder in a cul de sac unless we create more air.
Britain needs more air too. The real situa-

tion is that Britain must survive. She must be strong and must be great. In the councils of Europe and the councils of the world mother Britain can give a leadership that she has not given in recent years. This challenge now comes to Canada but we are faced with the fact, even in the speech from the throne, that Canada is not prepared to accept the challenge.
Emerson says that genius is not knowing more than another person, not being more knowledgeable, but rather the characteristic of acclimatizing oneself to the particular challenges and opportunities of the moment, and with common sense and wisdom taking advantage of these events and moments.
"Sterile" was the word originally used by the London Times to describe the negative attitude of the Prime Minister of Canada, and of his government throughout, with respect to developments far reaching in their consequences not only to Canada but to every human being in the world. Britain's entry into Europe can provide a depolarization of the world from the perilous situation where two great powers, Russia and United States might again lead us into a world war.
We believe in the north Atlantic community. It is a challenge and we believe that it will come to pass. We must face up to the opportunities it presents, and shape our economy to meet them. The Prime Minister was trying to draw an analogy between the exchange crisis so recently experienced by his government and the so-called crisis in 1947. I would remind the house that the crisis in 1947 arose because Canada, having poured out her material resources during the long years of the second world war, was then pouring out even more for the assistance of England, and thank God she did. Now the situation is that if Canada withdraws her strength and her power from Europe, from NATO and even from Britain she will obstruct England in her fight for survival.

Mr. Speaker, my first words will certainly be to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Chaplin and Mr. Vincent), who performed their tasks exceptionally well and said very interesting things.
Since the opening of this parliament, I have been given the opportunity of making a few observations and also a few comparisons with the time I was sitting in this house, that is from 1946 to 1949.
One often hears it said that years come and go but are not the same. I have found, since yesterday, that years do come and go and that they are often the same. While I

was here, in 1946, 1947 and 1948, things in this house were the other way around. The Liberals were sitting on the other side and the Conservatives, on this side.
When they were in opposition, the Conservatives spoke exactly like the Leader of the Opposition did for four hours without saying anything. The Conservatives who were then in opposition are now in power and they sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, and curiously enough, they are saying at this time exactly what the Liberal leaders were telling us in 1947, 1948 and 1949.
We are presented with a speech from the throne which should bring improvements to the lot of the Canadian people. Well, in that speech from the throne we see some projects outlined but no precision. Let us maintain austerity in a country as rich as Canada.
When have you ever seen, in Canada, a worm in a big apple starve to death because the apple was too big? When have you ever heard that, in a tropical country, a monkey on a banana tree starved to death because there were too many bananas on the tree?
And yet, here in Canada, where everything is plentiful-not one member in this house can say otherwise-there are 500,000 unemployed, and it is expected that their number will increase during the coming winter. We are told of misery in the midst of plenty.
When the Social Creditors ask for legislation that, instead of attacking private industry, instead of attacking the individual, would attack the financial system that does not take into account any of our country's physical possibilities, what do we hear? Statements of the kind we heard this afternoon: "Let us print more money. Let us print more money, without giving it any thought."
The matter was discussed not long after the elections on June 18, because after June 18 the Liberals and the Conservatives in Quebec held meetings to ask themselves: What is that Social Credit upsurge in the province of Quebec? Twenty six members here; 30 in all of Canada, but 26 from Quebec.
As I was saying, consideration was given to the upsurge of Social Credit. How could one account for the election of 26 Social Crediters?
I would gladly have suggested to both the Conservatives and the Liberals that they study the Social Credit doctrine itself instead of racking their brains. They would have seen what this is all about.
At this time, I should like to thank most sincerely the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) who has kindly relinquished 27507-3-10i
The Address-Mr. Caouette his time tonight because I must be in Montreal tomorrow. A thousand thanks to the hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, our country is undoubtedly extremely wealthy and yet, the Canadian people are constantly given the impression that it is absolutely impossible to develop our natural resources without foreign investments.
Now, there is nothing more stupid in my opinion than for our government to go around New York or Boston or elsewhere in the wide world, begging for leave to finance the development of our natural resources.
We have our wealth of natural resources, we have engineers, qualified personnel, labour force, we have men of good will, we have a Canadian society made up of all social classes, all prepared to undertake the development of our natural resources and increase our gross national product
We have all that, but because we lack financial authority to put everything into operation, we allow bankruptcies to occur increasingly in Canada, we allow thousands of unemployed to live in near squalor and we can find no solution to such a situation and when the Social Crediters submit their solutions we hear such comments as those made by a member of the opposition a moment ago: "Strike out the words Social Credit from your amendment to the amendment and we will be prepared to support it".
It is quite clear, if Social credit was taken out of the program, we would be sitting with the Liberals or the Conservatives. That is precisely why my friends and myself are sitting here, but after the next election-which will come too soon for the Leader of the Opposition

at the very first opportunity we shall sit across the aisle instead of this side.
The inconsiderate printing of money has never been part of the Social Credit platform, and hon. members in this house know it.
What we of the Social Credit party advocate is that there be as much money as products and services for consumers, that is all. To the extent that Canadians promote production, let the Bank of Canada print the necessary money to enable production to meet the needs of the people. That is common sense regardless of political allegiance.
The emphasis is on ever-increasing productivity, while we talk about greater productivity. At the same time, we notice that a

The Address-Mr. Caouette feeling of insecurity is growing everywhere in Canada. More and more, unemployment is plaguing our country. Everywhere, we hear the opposition, we hear the government, we hear our socialist friends preaching full employment: "A job for every Canadian". The more full employment is being talked about, the more automation and unemployment face us at home today.
What is the solution of the political parties, of the politicians and of the economists of Canada to the problem of automation now existing in our country and which will be called upon to play an increasingly important part in the next few years?
We are being told that it is a mathematical impossibility, a physical impossibility to create new jobs in the circumstances. Inasmuch as scientific progress replaces men in Canada, there is only one way to ensure the expansion of our industry: it is to give to the Canadian men, women and children a purchasing power which will allow them to buy the products of science, of machine, and of our industry. We shall therefore respect the human person, private property, private organizations, and private industries. At the same time we shall give to all Canadian citizens prosperity, security and freedom.
The problem of unemployment is not a problem of production or sentiment for Canadians, but a financial problem which is in the hands of consumers. When the consumers themselves will be able to finance an adequate national production, then we shall have security with greater freedom for each individual in Canada.
There is tight money in spite of unsuspected wealth; that is the result of the present system. Nobody dares attack the monetary system-yet it is that system which is defective. It is rather the individual who is attacked by debasing his personality. The human being is to be depersonalized.
There is more and more talk of economic planning. But when speaking of economic planning, many people-mostly those who are called ignorant-never have understood the country's economy. Those people believe in planning. It is my firm belief and deep conviction that it is not planning that we need in Canada, but rather money to allow us to do our own planning ourselves.
Let's take my own case. When I have money, I don't need the federal nor the provincial government to tell me what to do or

not to do. I am free to do what I please. Others are not more stupid than I am. The government is substituting itself to human personality and subjecting it to shackles and plans. It is precisely against such shackles and plans that we are fighting everywhere in Canada at present.
Not so long ago, a little boy told me after the election: "Mr. Caouette, come and see my new-born pups." So I went to that little boy's place and in a two by two box I saw seven puppies.
That's an old one.

As old as my friend, it amounts to practically the same thing.
In the corner, are the seven puppies with their eyes closed (like my friend of the Liberal party who has just interrupted me), because puppies do not open their eyes before nine or ten days. Those puppies, through instinct alone, could find their mother in the far corner of the box even with their eyes closed. Deprived of intelligence, they could nevertheless reach the source of abundance.
We are intelligent, our eyes are open, but we are unable to see the abundance in Canada. How can such a thing happen.
Mr. Speaker, I could have set up a government for the seven puppies, with a system of shackles and plans, and told the yellow puppy: "You shall not go to your mother immediately" or told the black puppy: "You shall go at such or such a time". I could have prevented them from ever reaching their mother in the other corner of the box. I could even have starved them to death. This is exactly what the Liberals gave us for 22 years and what the Conservatives are giving now.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Sure.
Do these puppies need money?

They use their instinct, while the hon. member has neither one nor the other.
(Translation):
And yet it was the Liberal leader, in 1935 the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, who said, and I quote:
(Text):
Once a nation has deprived itself of the control of its currency and credit it matters not who makes the law. When in control, usury will wreck any nation.
(Translation):
However, he never acted upon this solemn affirmation or declaration made in August, 1935, and it is for all these years that Social Credit, not only in Quebec but everywhere in Canada, has been asking for the return to

parliament of this sovereignty, concerning money and credit in Canada, and insists on the issuance of orders to the Bank of Canada to the effect that what is physically feasible and desirable for Canada should be made financially possible. When we have the opportunity and the physical capacity to do something, to develop our natural resources, let the question of money be subordinated to these possibilities and money itself be put to their use, instead of seeing them nullified or left untapped owing to the lack of funds and credit.
One often hears those who oppose Social Credit say that there is no lack of money in the country. They say no, there is enough money but it is not circulating fast enough. In fact, it is somewhat like a rabbit caught in a hollow log 16 feet long. The rabbit will run from one end of the log to the other and when he sees you at one end, he will run to the other end; if he sees someone there, he runs back to the other end. Then, you ask yourself this question: At what time or at what speed must the rabbit run inside the log so that he can be seen at both ends at the same time. That is the speed of circulation of money in Canada.
It is said that there is no shortage of money in Canada, but how is it possible that 85 per cent of the Canadian people borrow from finance companies on two, three, four and even five year terms?
In the field of housing, mortgages are granted for periods up to 35 years. If these people had enough cash, they would not have to borrow from finance companies at interest rates as high as 20, 25 and even 30 per cent or to mortgage their salaries for the next three years to buy this year's production.
In two or three years, we will still have to face another more serious problem, just because the problem of money and credit will not have been solved. We are of the opinion that many reforms are needed in Canada, but none of them will be possible as long as a monetary reform has not become a fact, as long as we have not succeeded in putting the Bank of Canada at the service of the Canadian people instead of having the Canadian people at the service of a money dictatorship.
Mr. Speaker, we feel that the only way to reform the money system in Canada, at the social, economic or political level, is to think mostly of the consumer not the producer. Goods are being produced but as I say, the
The Address-Mr. Caouette problem is that the consumer does not have the money to purchase the goods and services which are offered to him.
Why not tackle that problem and solve it once and for all? Afterwards, we could embark upon the necessary reforms at the economic and political levels, if you wish, and even at the social level, but the key to the problem remains the reform of the money system.
Some say that money is unimportant. No, money is not important for members of parliament and for big industries, but it still has some importance for most people. In a sense, money plays the role of a key in a door lock. If you wish to get inside a castle, the castle assuredly is more important than the key to it; however, if you do not have the key and the door is locked, you will simply be left standing outside. But on the other hand, if you hold the key with which to unlock the door, you will have access inside, and to the beauties of the castle, since the key will have done its job. Money should play exactly the same role in a well-organized and well-balanced economy.
Mr. Speaker, we hear people telling us of budget balance and balanced budgets. What does a balanced budget mean? What lies behind that? It is that the government decides not to spend more money than it has levied in taxes upon the people it governs and not to spend more than the total amount of tax collected at all levels. The economic activity of the country is thereby restricted, and instead of increasing the purchasing power up to the level of production, an effort is made to slow down production to the level of the buying power. By whom was this decision taken? By the majority of Canadian financiers who have exerted a great deal of influence. Everyone says that 75 to 80 per cent of the Canadian economy is in the hands of Americans, and yet we claim that we are a sovereign country in the free world.
We must regain possession of our rights and means of production through the agency of the Bank of Canada, a financial institution which belongs to the Canadian people. Let the Bank of Canada create credit at the same rate as the Canadian people produce goods and services.
We have recommended increased purchasing power not only during the electoral campaign but for the past 25 years in Quebec and for 30 years in the rest of the country. We have suggested various means of achieving

Division
this end. For example, the Leader of the Opposition repeated yesterday a suggestion already put forward by Social Crediters since 1945, that is to grant family allowances to all children who continue their studies until they are 21 years old. The Liberals have at least learned from Social Credit.
Then, we request the establishment through the Bank of Canada, of a new kind of credit based on the surplus of production over our total national revenue. Creation of that new source of credit through the Bank of Canada, would permit an increase of the old age security rates and its payment to those 65 or over, without means test and to those between 60 and 65, following a means test. This would permit a substantial increase of the old age pension which would allow our senior citizens to make a decent living in such a wealthy country as ours.
We also suggest an increase of family allowances proportionate to the cost of living.
Everybody knows that the cost of living has more than doubled since 1945 and that in 1956, family allowances were increased by the fabulous amount of $1 per child by the Liberals.
Mr. Speaker, we also suggest that no income tax be levied on any income of less than $5,000 a year. We, as members of the house, enjoy an almost identical exemption and we are quite happy about it. If that tax exemption is justified for members of parliament, it should also be justified for the voters who elected them last June 18.
Mr. Speaker, before closing, I wish to say to all members that we are in this parliament not only for one year but for several sessions. I am convinced that as soon as possible the whole of Canada will elect a Social Credit government which will put money to man's service. This is the wish I express before taking my seat.
